The general rule was to give 30,000 steps to runs outside the transition
region, but when such points failed to be validly in equilibrium, they
were run between 100K and 300K steps. Points in the transition region
were slated to run about 4M steps, but some fell slightly short for
various reasons. @fig-S3steps shows the total steps vs. total energy per
particle for series 3.

# Specific Heat

The specific heat is the slope of the energy vs. temperature curve.

```{r}
#| label: fig-EvT
#| fig-cap: "The total energy vs. temperature.  The dotted line is attempting to show the very small standard deviation of the energy points.  The red triangles are points not considered validly inequilibrium. Remember that the temperature data has significant standard deviations, but these are not displayed."
setkey( S3DTdiff2, ke.mean.rs)
plotconfMD2( x='ke.mean.rs', y="TE", 
             df=S3DTdiff2[ TE.mean.rs %within% c(0.135,0.155)],
             linethresh=200, xlab="Kinetic Energy per Particle", 
             ylab ="Total Energy per Particle")# sets up plot
```

We need a numerical derivative function in order to compute
$C_v = dE / dT$. We will simply fit (really, *draw*) a line or curve
between a number of points, and compute the derivative of that line or
curve. `lm( y ~ poly( x, n), ...)` will fit a polynomial of degree `n`
to the values passed it, and if we pass `n + 1` values, the fit will be
exact (i.e., pass through the supplied points). The derivative will be
evaluated at the midpoint between the first and last point.

```{r}
#| label: dydx

dydx <- function( y, x, lag = 1) {
   # find derivative over lag + 1 points
   lx <- length( x)
   stopifnot( length( y) == lx)
   data <- data.table( x = x, y = y, keyby = x)
   xm <- (data$x[ 1:(lx - lag)] + data$x[ (lag + 1):lx]) / 2 # midpoint of eval sets
   dydxfit <- function( i) { # get dy/dx from points i:(i + lag)
      c <- coef( lm( y ~ poly( x, lag, raw = TRUE), # get poly coef
                     data = data[ i:(i + lag)]))
      dpc <- (1:lag) * tail( c, -1) # derivative of poly coeff
      polyval( rev(dpc), xm[ i]) # evaluate polynomial at midpoint of data & return
   }
   dd <- vapply( 1:(lx - lag), dydxfit, 1.0)
   list( dd=dd, xm = xm)
}

# test
tx <- c(1, 4, 3, 3.5, 2, 5)
ty <- tx^2
(dd <- dydx(ty, tx, 2)) # Note the NaN in third position: 3,  5, NaN, 7, 9
dd$dd - 2 * dd$xm
rm( tx, ty, dd) # remove these variables
```

The negative values are unrealistic, but not unsurprising due to the
fluctuations in the transition region. While the line looks pretty flat,
it also looks like it is zero, which is clearly a scaling issue: the
large values returned by the first difference causes the variations in
the rest of the line to be unnoticeable. We can also exclude the points
not considered valid, and this generates all positive results, and with
one very large value, so a log plot is used in @fig-Cv2.

# Transtion Statistics

## Deviation from the Mean Detection

We need a function which will find when a statistic departs from its
mean value (i.e., a step in the statistic).

```{r}
#| label: stepdet
stepdet <- function( x, nsig = 3, nstart = 10) {
  # x is a numeric vector
  # nsig is the number of standard deviations from the running mean x[i] must
  # \depart to be considered a step.
  # nstart is the number of points to start the running mean.
  # x <- x[ !is.na(x)] # drop any NA values before length test.
  stopifnot( length( x) > nstart +1)
  
  cumdet <- function( state, new){
    # state is a list with the following elements:
    #   sx: cumsum of x
    #   ss: the sum of squares
    #   n: the number of points in the running mean
    #   nv: the count when first detected
    # new is a new value to add to the running mean.
    if (state$nv == 0 ) { # only do this if we haven't detected a departure
      meanx <- state$sx / state$n 
      sdx <- sqrt( (state$ss - state$n * meanx^2)/ (state$n - 1)) 
      #print(state)
      #print( c( meanx, sdx))
      if( abs( new - meanx) < (nsig * sdx)) { # nothing detected
        state$sx <- state$sx + new
        state$ss <- state$ss + new^2
        state$n <- state$n + 1
        state$nv <- 0
      } else { # departure detected
        state$nv <- state$n + 1
      }
    } # simply return state.
    return( state)
  }
  sxs <- sum( x[ 1:nstart])
  sss <- sum( x[ 1:nstart]^2) #sum squared start.
  s <- list( sx = sxs, ss = sss, n = nstart, nv = 0)
  #print( s)
  Reduce( cumdet, x[(nstart + 1):length( x)], init = s)
}

(testcumdet <- stepdet( tx <- c( rnorm(20), 5 + rnorm(10))))
```

This works quite well to detect the start of diffusion (@fig-diffdet).

```{r}
#| label: fig-diffdet
#| fig-cap: "Detecting the start of diffusion.  The red dashed line is the temperature at which the $3\\sigma$ detection threshold is crossed.  The blue line is the mean value of the points preceding the detection. Black circles are points considered valid, and red triangles not valid. Blue band indicates the standard error of the estimates."
detects <- c( detects, 
              diff = with( S3DTdiff2[ !is.na( nrd),], {
  ps <- stepdet( Estimated)
  kedet <- ke.mean.rs[ ps$nv]
  cat( run[ ps$nv], ", T = ", ke.mean.rs[ ps$nv], ", 4D = ", 
       Estimated[ ps$nv], "\n", sep = '')
  plotconf( y = Estimated, x = ke.mean.rs, panel.first = grid(), Fval = Fval, 
            xlab = "ke", ylab = "4D", sd = Std.Errord,
            main = "Diffusion vs. Temperature, Detection of Diffusion Start",
            xlim = c(0.01, 0.015), ylim = c(0.0, 0.05))
  abline( v = kedet, col = 'red', lty = 2)
  mx = ps$sx / ps$n
  cat( "Mean of points before crossing: ", mx, "\n")
  abline( h = mx, col = 'darkblue', lty = 1)
  kedet
}))
rpl <- recordPlot()
png( "diffvkez.png", width = 600, height = 300)
replayPlot( rpl)
invisible( dev.off())
detectsex <- c( detectsex, diff = "Start of diffusion (stepdet)." )
```

Note that there are two hotter points with very low diffusion, one valid
and one not. We can also detect with the F statistic (which for all
these diffusion data has 1 and 8 degrees of freedom). @fig-Fvke shows
the F statistic vs. temperature.

```{r}
#| label: fig-Fvke
#| fig-cap: "F statistic vs. temperature. The red triangles are the points not considered valid. Solid black line is $F=1$."
with( S3DTdiff2[ !is.na( nrd),], {
   plotconf( x = ke.mean.rs, y = Fvald, 
            panel.first = grid(), Fval = Fval, 
            xlab = "ke", ylab = "F stat.", log = 'y',
            main = "Diff. Regression F vs. Temperature")
})
abline( h = 1.0)
```

We can see in the above a sharp break. There are four points with $F$
statistics above one but less than 10. @tbl-DiffFvals shows the runs
meeting that criteria.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-DiffFvals
#| tbl-cap: "Diffusion regressions with $F$-values between one and ten."

knitr::kable( S3DTdiff2[Fvald %within% c(1,10), 
                        .(run, valid, ke.mean.rs, Fvald, Fpvalued, Estimated)])
```

The first (the coldest point) has a negative regression line, even
though it's F statistic is almost four (3.82, p-value is
`r S3DTdiff2[run == "S3.0001", Fpvalued]`, so pretty significant, except
that it is diffusing backward, whatever that might mean). The second one
is run `S3.0026`, whose diffusion F statistic is just over one, for an
insignificant p-value of `r S3DTdiff2[run == "S3.0026", Fpvalued]`, and
a diffusion value within the range of the non-diffusing points
(`r S3DTdiff2[run == "S3.0026", Estimated]`). The other two are likely
hot enough to be diffusing, but the regressions are unconvincing. Note
that the 95% confidence $F$-value for 1 and 8 degrees of freedom is
above 5 (`r qf( 0.95, 1, 8)`).

Ultimately we will use the signifcance value (the `Fpvalued` column) to
detect the start of diffusion. @fig-Fpvke shows the F statistic p-value
vs. temperature, and we will use a p-value of 0.01 (99% confidence) to
detect the start of diffusion.

```{r}
#| label: fig-Fpvke
#| fig-cap: "F statistic p- value vs. temperature. The solid black line shows the 99% significance threshold (p-value of 0.01). The vertical red dashed line is the coldest point showing diffusion.  The red triangles are the points not considered valid."
detects <- c(detects, diffpval = with( S3DTdiff2[ !is.na( nrd),], {
   plotconf( x = ke.mean.rs, y = Fpvalued, 
            panel.first = grid(), Fval = Fval, 
            xlab = "ke", ylab = "p-val", log = 'y',
            main = "Diff. Regression p-value vs. Temperature",
            #xlim = c(0.01, 0.015)) 
            #ylim = ylim = c(0.0, 0.05))
   )
   diffp <- ke.mean.rs[Fpvalued < 0.01][1]
   abline( v = diffp, col = 'red', lty = 2)
   diffp
}))
detectsex <- c( detectsex, diffpval = "First point with p-value below 0.01 (99% confidence)")
abline( h = 0.01)
```

The pressure and temperature curves require us to detect the change of
slope. Use of the `dydx()` function might seem appropriate, but with
noisy data and unevenly spaced `x` values, we can get large departures
from mean values just due to noise.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ddPress
#| fig-cap: "Estimated derivative of the pressure data, plotted on a logarithmic scale (three values were negative so absolute value is plotted). The red dashed line marks where the $7\\sigma$ detection linear threshold was crossed.  Thresholds lower than $7\\sigma$ would be crossed by noise at lower temperatures (found emperically)."
ddpt <- dydx( y = S3DTdiff2$Pressure.mean.rs, x = S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs)
ps <- stepdet( ddpt$dd, nsig = 7)
col = rep( 'blue', length( ddpt$dd))
col[ (ps$n + 1):length( col)] <- 'red'
plot( y = abs( ddpt$dd), x = ddpt$xm, col = col, log = 'y', 
      panel.first = grid(), 
      xlab = "T", ylab = "<dP/dT>", 
      main = "Derivative of Pressure vs. Temperature")
abline( v = ddpt$xm[ ps$nv + 1], col = 'red', lty = 2)
mx = ps$sx / ps$n
sdx = sqrt( (ps$ss - ps$n * mx^2) / (ps$n - 1))
cat( ps$n, ps$nv, ddpt$dd[ ps$nv], mx, sdx, mx + 5 * sdx, mx - 5 * sdx, "\n")
abline( h = mx, col = 'darkblue', lty = 1)
detects <- c( detects, dPdT = ddpt$xm[ ps$nv])
detectsex <- c( detectsex, dPdT = "Estimated dPdT detection." )
```

Below in @fig-diffPress we try the simple first difference of the
pressure data, and it takes a $5\sigma$ threshold to get a dependable
detection.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diffPress
#| fig-cap: "First difference of the pressure data.  The red dashed line is the $5\\sigma$ detection threshold crossing.  The blue line is the mean of points before the crossing, and the dashed lines are the $\\pm 5\\sigma$ limits."
prdf <- diff( S3DTdiff2$Pressure.mean.rs)
ps <- stepdet( prdf, nsig=5)
kedet <- S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs[ ps$nv + 1] # +1 because of diff
S3DTdiff2[ ps$nv, .( run, Pressure.mean.rs, ke.mean.rs)]
col = rep( 'blue', length( prdf))
col[ (ps$nv):length( prdf)] <- 'red'
plot( y = prdf, x = tail( S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs, -1), xlim=c(0.0, 0.015),
      main = "First difference of Pressure vs. Temperature",
      col = col, panel.first = grid(), xlab = "ke", ylab = "diff(Pressure)")
abline( v = kedet, col = 'red', lty = 2)
mx = ps$sx / ps$n # mean of points before crossing
sdx = sqrt( (ps$ss - ps$n * mx^2) / (ps$n - 1)) # STD. DEV of points bfr xing
abline( h = mx, col = 'darkblue', lty = 1)
abline( h = mx - 5 * sdx, col = 'darkblue', lty = 2)
abline( h = mx + 5 * sdx, col = 'darkblue', lty = 2)
detects <- c( detects, diffP = kedet)
detectsex <- c( detectsex, 
                diffP = "Detection on first difference of Isochor data." )
```

## Linear Detection

This isn't satisfactory. A function that will fit a line to the data and
detect when the next point departs significantly from the line is
needed.

```{r}
#| label: linedet
linedet <- function( x, y, level = 0.99, nstart = 10) {
  # x & y are a numeric vectors of the same length
  # nsig is the probability that a noise deviation will cause a false detection
  #   over the total run of points.
  # depart to be considered a step.
  # nstart is the number of points to start the running mean.
  lx <- length( x)
  stopifnot( lx > nstart +1)
  stopifnot( lx == length( y))
  dt <- data.table( x = x, y = y)
  for ( i in nstart:lx) { # step through looking for a departure
    pr <- predict( lm( y ~ x, data = dt[ 1:i,]), 
                   newdata = data.frame( x = x[ i + 1]), 
                   interval = "prediction", level = level)
    # cat( i, pr, "\n")
    if (!(y[ i + 1] %within% pr[, c("lwr","upr")])) { # if departure detected
      return( c( nv = i + 1, x = x[ i + 1], y = y[ i + 1],
                 pred = pr[1, 1], lwr = pr[1, 2], upr = pr[1, 3]))
      } # if (!(y...)
  } # for ( i...)
}

tx <- 1:30
ty <- tx + rnorm(30)
ty[ 21:30] <- ty[ 21:30] + 5
(testcumdet <- linedet( x = tx, y = ty))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
rm( tx, ty, testcumdet) # remove test variables.
```

We can try this on the isochor data (@fig-isochf1).

```{r}
#| label: fig-isochf1
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: Isochor of points up to first detection, plus ten points.  Red vertical dashed line shows the detected point.
(pr1 <- linedet(  x = S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs, y = S3DTdiff2$Pressure.mean.rs, 
                 level = 0.99))
kedet <- unname( pr1[ "x"])
model1 <- lm( Pressure.mean.rs ~ ke.mean.rs, 
             data = S3DTdiff2[ 1:(pr1["nv"] - 1),])
plotconfMD2( x = "ke.mean.rs", y = "Pressure", xlab = "T", 
             main = "Isochor of points up to first detection",
             df = S3DTdiff2[ 1:(pr1["nv"] + 10),])
abline( v = kedet, col = 'red', lty = 2)
lines( S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs[1:(pr1["nv"] - 1)], 
       predict( model1, interval="prediction", level = 0.99)[, "upr"], 
       col = "blue")
text( x = kedet, y = pr1["y"], labels = "icld1", pos = 4, cex = 0.8)
text( x = kedet, y = pr1["y"], labels = format( kedet, width = 5), pos = 2, 
      cex = 0.8)
grid()
detects <- c( detects, icld1 = kedet) # isochor linedet 1
detectsex <- c( detectsex, icld1 = "Isochore linedet detection at 0.99." )
```

That is a surprise. Note how tight the prediction interval is: $\pm$
`r 100 * (pr1["upr"] - pr1["lwr"]) / (2 * pr1["pred"])`% of the
prediction. This is a result of the data being tightly clustered around
the regression line up through the 15th point. The 16th point departs
above the 99.99 percentile (@fig-fit1resid).

```{r}
#| label: fig-fit1resid
#| fig-cap: "Residuals of the 15 point regression plotted to the first _16_ points. Blue dotted line is the 99% prediction interval, and the red dotted line is the 99.99% interval."
x1 <- S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs[ 1:pr1["nv"]] # all points including detected.
y1 <- predict( model1, newdata = data.frame( ke.mean.rs = x1), 
               interval = "prediction", level = 0.99)
plot( x = x1, y = (S3DTdiff2$Pressure.mean.rs[ 1:pr1["nv"]] - y1[, 'fit']), 
      xlab = "T", ylab = "P - Pred(Pressure)", 
      main = "Pressure Residuals vs. Temperature", panel.first = grid())
lines( x1, y1[,"upr"] - y1[, 'fit'], col = 'blue', lty = 2)
y2 <- predict( model1, newdata = data.frame( ke.mean.rs = x1), 
               interval = "prediction", level = 0.9999)
lines( x1, y2[,"upr"] - y2[, 'fit'], col = 'red', lty = 2)
abline( h = 0.0)
```

The first 15 points make a tight linear model, but the 16th point makes
a significant deviation beyond the 99.99% interval. The linear detection
seemed to work pretty well, and the plot shows that the fitted points
are holding no trends. While we can clearly see where the linear trend
ends, the data gets increasingly noisy as the substance heats beyond
$T=0.008$. Various detection thresholds will continue to detect other
breaks that are of no obvious significance. @fig-isochf2 shows that five
nines (99.999%) are needed to skip to the obvious departure near
$T=0.0128$.

In order to complete the analysis, we should label each point, meaning
we need to identify the fully fluid region and the transition region.
Let's run the detection in reverse (@fig-isochf4) to find the start of
the fluid region.

```{r}
#| label: fig-isochf4
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: Detection of Isochor points in reverse.  The fit is not nearly so good (the fluid phase pressure, which has the most points, is not linear in temperature), but the detector works nevertheless. The dashed red verticle lines delinate the start of the transition region, and the start of the fluid regions.
setorder( S3DTdiff2, -ke.mean.rs) # This will order the data in reverse.
(pr4 <- linedet( x = S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs, y = S3DTdiff2$Pressure.mean.rs, 
                 level = 0.99))
# Since this is in reverse, we need to adjust the point number.
pr4["nv"] <- nrow(S3DTdiff2) - pr4["nv"] + 2 
# +2 to make the point the left-most point of the fluid region. 
# +1 would put in in the transition region.
setkey( S3DTdiff2, ke.mean.rs) # restore the original order.
kedet4 <- S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs[ pr4["nv"]]
rng <- pr4["nv"]:nrow(S3DTdiff2) # range of points to use
model4 <- lm( Pressure.mean.rs ~ ke.mean.rs, data = S3DTdiff2[ rng,])
plot( Pressure.mean.rs ~ ke.mean.rs,  data = S3DTdiff2, typ ="b",
      xlim = c( 0.01, .015), ylim = c( 0.10, 0.115),
      xlab = "Temperature", ylab = "Pressure"
      )

lines( S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs[rng], 
       predict( model4, interval = "prediction", level = 0.99)[, "fit"], 
       col = "blue")
lines( S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs[rng], 
       predict( model4, interval = "prediction", level = 0.99)[, "lwr"], 
       col = "blue", lty=2)
lines( S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs[rng], 
       predict( model4, interval = "prediction", level = 0.99)[, "upr"], 
       col = "blue", lty=2)
grid()
#text(x=S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs[rng], y=S3DTdiff2$Pressure.mean.rs[rng], 
#     labels = format( S3DTdiff2$Pressure.mean.rs[rng], wdth = 5), pos = 4, 
#     cex = 0.8)
detects <- c( detects, icld4 = kedet4) # isochor linedet 3
detectsex <- c( detectsex, icld4 = "Isochore linedet in reverse (high temp)")
detects[ c("icld1", "icld2", "icld3", "icld4")]
abline( v = detects[ c("icld1", "icld2", "icld3", "icld4")], col = 'red', 
        lty = 2)

```

The data can be tagged with the detected state. We will distinguish two
solid states, a transition state, and a fluid state.

```{r}
#| label: fig-State
#| fig-cap: Isochor with points colored by state.
#| warning: false
S3DTdiff2[ , State := cut( ke.mean.rs, labels = c("Solid1", "Solid2", 
                                                  "Transition", "Fluid"),
            breaks = c( 0, detects[ c("icld1", "icld3", "icld4")], 100),
            right = FALSE)]
plot( Pressure.mean.rs ~ ke.mean.rs,  data = S3DTdiff2, col = State,
      xlim = c( 0.006, .017), ylim = c( 0.095, 0.115),
      xlab = "T", ylab = "Pressure")
grid()
legend( "bottomright", #col = S3DTdiff2$State, 
        legend = levels(S3DTdiff2$State), pch = 1, col = 1:4,
        title = "State")
model5 <- lm( Pressure.mean.rs ~ ke.mean.rs * State, data = S3DTdiff2)
summary( model5)
```

This is not exactly what I expected. The model does a good job of
containing the data, even though the fluid region is clearly non-linear
in ke (@fig-isochf5).

```{r}
#| label: fig-isochf5
#| warning: false
tp1 <- predict( model5, interval = "prediction", level=0.99)
plotconfMD2( S3DTdiff2, x = "ke.mean.rs", y = "Pressure",
             xlim = c( 0.006, .017), ylim = c( 0.095, 0.115))
lines( x=S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs, y=tp1[,"fit"], col='red')
lines( x=S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs, y=tp1[,"lwr"], col='red', lty=2)
lines( x=S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs, y=tp1[,"upr"], col='red', lty=2)
```

Modeling just the solid state as two regions will compare just those two
regions.

```{r}
model6 <- lm( Pressure.mean.rs ~ ke.mean.rs * State, 
              data = S3DTdiff2[ State %in% c("Solid1", "Solid2"),])
summary( model6)
```

That states that the two solid regions have statistically different
specific heats, to a virtual certainty. The model above is
$P = \alpha_0 + \beta_0 T + s(\alpha_s +\beta_s T)$, where $s$ is one in
the `Solid2` state and zero otherwise, and $\alpha_0$, $\beta_0$,
$\alpha_s$, and $\beta_s$ are the coefficients of the model. The
calculation below shows that the coefficients above apply to that form
of the equation.

```{r}
#| label: cm6
cm6 <- coef( model6)
with( S3DTdiff2[ State %in% c("Solid1", "Solid2")], {
   Temp <- ke.mean.rs # use kinetic energy as temperature
   P <- Pressure.mean.rs
   s <- as.numeric( State == "Solid2") # 1 if Solid2, 0 otherwise
   pred <- cm6[1] + cm6[2] * Temp + s * (cm6[3] + cm6[4] * Temp)
   sum( pred - predict( model6)) # should be zero
   #plot( Pressure.mean.rs ~ ke.mean.rs, col = State,
})
```

The code below shows that `model6` (which estimates $\beta_s$) is a
significantly better fit than `model2`.

```{r}
#| label: anova26
anova( model2, model6)
AIC( model2, model6)
```

So model 6 (the only one to estimate $\beta_s$ is clearly superior to
almost ten 9's (99.99...99%) certainty. The actual value of the specific
heats can be best garnered from the coefficients of the models of just
those sections (see @tbl-models1). The intercepts are not important and
so not presented in the table (most are available in the code output
above).

| Model | Data | $\beta_0 \pm \sigma_\beta$ ($\beta_s \pm \sigma_{\beta_s}$) |
|----|----|----|
| model1 | `Solid1` | 1.104 $\pm0.04\%$ |
| model2 | `Solid1` & `Solid2` | 1.122 $\pm0.26\%$ |
| model3 | `Solid2` | 1.162 $\pm0.54\%$ |
| model6 | `Solid1` & `Solid2` | 1.104 $\pm0.22\%$, (0.0574 $\pm 8.2\%$) |

: Significant model fits. All slope coefficients were highly
significant. Model 2 included both solid regions, but treated them as as
one block of data. Model 4 (fluid region) and model 5 (linear model of
all four states) are not relevant to these results. {#tbl-models1}

The `model6` coefficients for `Solid2` (where the two are added) differ
from that estimated in `model3` by only
`r 100*(cm6["ke.mean.rs"] + cm6["ke.mean.rs:StateSolid2"] - coef(model2)["ke.mean.rs"])/coef(model3)["ke.mean.rs"]`%.

## Summary Statistics

We will plot the various statistics and draw some lines where melting
begins.

```{r}
#| label: trlines
S3DTdiff2[ , ':='( rv = ke.sd.rs / ke.mean.rs)] # add relative variance column
setkey( S3DTdiff2, ke.mean.rs) # ensure data is sorted by temperature
# Next line will select the first run with a P-value < 0.01:
# i.e., highly probably regression.
(mdiff <- S3DTdiff2[ Fpvalued < 0.01, ke.mean.rs][1])
# run with highest relative variance
(kesd <-  S3DTdiff2[ which.max( S3DTdiff2$rv), ke.mean.rs]) 
detects <- c( detects, mdiff = mdiff, 
              rvmax = S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs[ which.max( S3DTdiff2$rv)])
detectsex <- c( detectsex, mdiff = "First diffusion with correlation.",
                rvmax = "Max relative variance")
```

First, we need to `melt()` the data table.

```{r}
#| label: S3DTd2m
# First select just the columns we're interested in
S3DTd2ss <- S3DTdiff2[,.( run, Temp = ke.mean.rs, rv, LogFp = log(Fpvalued), 
                          D = Estimated / 4.0, 
                          TE = TE.mean.rs,
                          valid = fifelse( valid == 1, TRUE, FALSE), psiavg,
                          psiabs.mean.rs, Pressure = Pressure.mean.rs)]
id.var = c( "run", "Temp", "valid")
S3DTd2m <- melt( S3DTd2ss, id.var = id.var, direction = 'long') 
# now each variable is its own table.
# The following will create a table of Log(Cv) values.
Cvlen <- length( dedt1$xm) 
CvTable <- data.table( run = rep( "0", Cvlen), 
                       valid = fifelse( dedt1$xm %within% c( 0.01283, 0.014095),
                                        FALSE, TRUE), 
                       Temp = dedt1$xm, variable = rep( "Log(Cv)", Cvlen),
                       value = log( dedt1$dd))
S3DTd2m2 <- rbind( S3DTd2m, CvTable)
head( S3DTd2m2)
```

Frankly not sure why that worked (I don't understand exactly what
`id.var = id.var` or `varying` does), but we now have each run with its
temperature, and the *value* of each variable.

@fig-Transition below shows plots of eight statistics. The Log of the
specific heat calculated across the whole data set as `lag = 1`;
estimates using points where the temperature is not considered valid
have been plotted with blue dots. TE is total energy, `rv` is the
relative temperature variance (the variance of the 500-point re-sampled
temperatures divided by the temperature mean), `psiavg` is the magnitude
of the average of $\psi$ (i.e., the step-by-step average of the complex
quantity) and `psiabs.mean.rs` is the step-by-step average of the
magnitude of $\psi$. `D` is the estimate of diffusion computed as,
`LogFp` is the natural log of the probability of F-value of the
diffusion regression of $\left< R^2(t) \right> \sim t$ (where $t$ is
time;). Low probabilities indicate that that the regression line was
unlikely caused by random noise, and thus diffusion was present.
`Log(Cv)` is the natural logarithm of the estimated specific heat, which
is computed as the first difference of the total energy divided by the
temperature. The vertical red dashed lines mark the detected
transitions.

```{r}
#| label: fig-Transition
#| fig-cap: "Statistics around transition plotted against temperature. Tan dots are points considered valid, blue ones not valid.  See text for description of statistics. Verticle red dashed lines are mark the transition detections." 
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-width: 6.5
xlim <- c(0.0069, 0.016)
xyplot( value ~ Temp | variable, 
        data = S3DTd2m2[ Temp %within% xlim,], groups = valid, 
        #layout = c( 0, 7), 
        pch = c(16, 16), 
        #auto.key = list(space = "right", pch=c(16,16)),
        scales=list( y = list( relation = "free")),
        xlab = "Temperature",
        Main = "Key Series Three Statistics Around Transition",
        #par.settings = simpleTheme(pch = c(16, 16), 
        #       col = c("peru", "cornflowerblue")),
        panel = function(...) {
           panel.xyplot(...)
           panel.grid( h=-1, v=-1)
           panel.abline( v = detects, col = "red" , lty = 2)
         })
rpl <- recordPlot()
png("Transitions.png", width = 6.5, height = 9, units = "in", res = 100)
replayPlot(rpl)
invisible( dev.off())
```

@tbl-detects shows the detected transitions plotted as vertical lines in
@fig-Transition and their descriptions.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-detects
#| tbl-cap: "Detected transition temperatures and their descriptions. All of the points except for the Cv (specific heat) and dPdT are the mean kinetic energy per paricle of a particular run. Estimates using the `dydx` function can report temperatures between runs."
detdt <- data.table( T = detects, Names = names(detects), Desc. = detectsex)
setkey( detdt, T)
knitr::kable( detdt)
```

# Summary

As can be seen in @fig-Transition and @tbl-detects, that, excepting the
first, most the detected transition points are either close or the same.
The value `r detects['mdiff']` is from run `S3.00275`. The next colder
detection is the `dPdT` whose temperature is between runs `S3.00275` and
`S3.0026`. The hottest detected point (`maxCv2`) is not to be trusted,
as it is based only on "valid" points. While the "not valid" points were
showing signs of sloping temperatres with time, those slopes were very
small, and that technique excludes so many points that the estimated
temperature of the max Cv has a wide expected variance (not computed
here).

The Nelson-Halperin order parameter $\psi$ and the diffusion are very
different measures of the same thing. @fig-psivD shows $\psi$ plotted
against the logarithm of the diffusion estimate $D$. Both are reliable
estimates of the state of the substance.

```{r}
#| label: fig-psivD
#| fig-cap: Nelson-Halperin order parameter plotted agains the natural logarithm of the diffusion estimate. Red triangles are "not valid" points.
with( S3DTdiff2, 
      plotconf( y = psiavg, x = log( abs( Estimated / 4)), Fval = Fval,
                xlab = "D", ylab = expression(psi),
                main = "Comparing order parameter and diffusion")
)
```

No evidence of a second transition was found.

## Isotherm and Isobar

We will start be reproducing the isochor plot of all points
(@fig-pvske_eta). The isochor is a plot of pressure vs. temperature
(constant density).

The $r^{-n}$ potential allows us to create isobars (constant pressure)
or isotherms (constant temperature) from constant density data. The
important thermodynamic variable is
$\eta = \rho \sigma^2 \left( \epsilon / k T \right)^{2/n}$, where $\rho$
is the density, $T$ is the temperature, and $\sigma$, $\epsilon$ and $k$
are the distance unit, energy unit, and Boltzmann's constant
respectively, all are defined as one, meaning $\rho$ and $T$ are in
scaled units [@Shea1980] [@Novaco1982].

```{r}
#| label: fig-pvske_eta
#| eval: true
#| output: true
#| fig-cap: 'Isochor of all points at density $\rho = 1/\pi$. The blue dashed lines represent the temperature and pressure of the isotherm and isobar plots below.  The gray lines are lines of constant $\eta = \rho \left( \epsilon / T \right)^{2/n}$.'
isotherm <- function( P1, T1, T2, n) {P1 * (T2 / T1)^(1 + 2/n)} # compute P2
isot = 0.0129
isob = 0.1075
plotconfMD2( S3DTdiff2, x = "ke.mean.rs", y = "Pressure", 
             xlab = "Temperature", ylab = "Pressure",
             main = "Isochor of all points with scaling lines", 
            ylim = c( 0.01, 0.15))
abline( h = isob, col= "blue", lty = 2)
abline( v = isot, col= "blue", lty = 2)
  tr <- range( S3DTdiff2$ke.mean.rs) # T1 range
  ts <- seq( tr[1], tr[2], length.out = 200)
  t1s <- isot + c(-0.005, -0.01, 0, 0.005, 0.01, 0.015, 0.02,.025, .03)
  for (T1 in t1s) {
    lines( x = ts, y = isotherm( isob, T1, ts, 5), col = 'gray', lty = 1, 
           lwd = 2)
  }
  pl <- recordPlot()
png("pvske_eta.png", width=600, height=300)
replayPlot(pl)
invisible(dev.off())
```

The scaling lines show that when scaling to constant pressure,
temperatures below the constant pressure scale up in temperature, and
those above scale down. Conversely, when scaling to constant
temperature, pressures below the constant temperature scale up in
pressure, and those above scale down, both rather dramatically.

The pressure and temperature scale such that
$P_1 / \rho_1 T_1 = P_2 / \rho_2 T_2$ (this is the equivalent of the
[Ideal Gas Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_gas_law) in two
dimensions). If we want to draw an isobar or isotherm curve, we need use
the scaling to map the measurements to different scales. If we have a
measurement $T_1$ and pressure $P_1$ at density $\rho_1$ ($1/\pi$ for
us), we can map $T_2$ to a pressure $P_2$ via

$$
T_2 = \frac{\rho_1 T_1 P_2}{\rho_2 P_1}
$$

Then we use $\eta = \rho_1 / T_1^{2/n} = \rho_2 / T_2^{2/n}$ to replace
$\rho_2 = \rho_1 \left(T_2/ T_1\right)^{2/n}$ in the above yielding

\begin{align*}
T_2 &= \frac{\rho_1 T_1 P_2}{P_1 \eta T_2^{2/n}} \\
    &= \frac{\rho_1 T_1 P_2}{ P_1 \left(\rho_1 / T_1^{2/n}\right) T_2^{2/n}} \\
T_2^{1 + 2/n} &= \frac{T_1^{1 + 2/n} P_2}{P_1} \\
T_2 &= T_1 \left( P_2/P_1 \right)^{\left( 1 / (1 + 2/n) \right)}\\
    &= T_1 \left( \frac{P_2}{P_1} \right)^{\left( n/ (n + 2) \right)}
\end{align*}

That's messy, but now that we have a $T_2$. Then we use
$\rho_2 = \rho_1 \left( T_2 / T_1 \right)^{2/n}$ to compute a new
density. @fig-isobar2507 shows the isobar at $P=0.1075$, which is near
the transition at $1/\pi$ density (see @fig-pvske_eta).

```{r}
#| label: fig-isobar2507
#| eval: true
#| output: true
#| fig-cap: 'Isobar at $P=0.1075$, the pressure near the transition at $1/\pi$ density (see @fig-pvske_eta).'
with( S3DTdiff2, {
  n <- 5 # current potential exponent
  P2 <- isob # near transition pressure at 1/pi density
  T2 <- ke.mean.rs * (P2 / Pressure.mean.rs)^(n / (n + 2))
  den2 <- (1 / pi) * (T2 / ke.mean.rs)^(2/n)
  plotconf( x = (1 / den2), y = T2, Fval = Fval, linethresh = 200, 
            panel.first = grid(), xlab = "Area / Particle", 
            ylab = "Temperature", 
            main = " Isobar at P = 0.1075"#xlim = c( 3.0, 3.5)
            )
  axis( side = 1, at = pi, labels = expression(pi))
})
pl <- recordPlot()
png("isobar2507.png", width=600, height=300)
replayPlot(pl)
invisible(dev.off())
```

Similar algebra yields the following for a constant temperature
(Isotherm). Since we are transforming to a constant temperature, we can
first compute the new density
$\rho_2 = \rho_1 \left( T_2 / T_1 \right)^{2/n}$. Then:

\begin{align*}
P_2 &= \frac{P_1 \rho_2 T_2}{\rho_1 T_1} \\
    &= \frac{P_1 \eta T_2^{1 + 2/n}}{\rho_1 T_1} \\
    &= \frac{P_1 \left(\rho_1 / T_1^{n/2}\right)T_2^{1 + 2/n} }{\rho_1 T_1} \\
    &= P_1 \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^{1 + 2/n}
\end{align*}

If we have pre-computed the new density, we can stop at the first step
above, but sometimes we don't care about the density, and so the final
form is utilized. The code below generates @fig-isotherm2507.

```{r}
#| label: fig-isotherm2507
#| eval: true
#| output: true
#| fig-cap: 'Isotherm in the tranistion region.'
with( S3DTdiff2, {
  n <- 5 # current potential exponent
  #P2 <- Pressure.mean.rs * (T2 / ke.mean.rs)^(1 + 2/n)
  den2 <- (1 / pi) * (isot / ke.mean.rs)^(2/n)
  P2 <- isotherm( Pressure.mean.rs, ke.mean.rs, isot, n) # compute P2
  plotconf( x = (1/den2), y = P2, Fval = Fval, linethresh = Inf, 
            panel.first = grid(), xlab = "Area / Particle", ylab = "Pressure", 
            xlim = c( 2.8, 3.5), ylim = c(0.08, .15), 
            main = "Isotherm at T = 0.0129"
            )
  axis( side = 1, at = pi, labels = expression(pi))
  # compare two methods to compute P2:
  sum( (Pressure.mean.rs * den2 * pi * (isot / ke.mean.rs) - P2)^2)
})
pl <- recordPlot()
png("isotherm2507.png", width=600, height=300)
replayPlot(pl)
invisible(dev.off())
```

With temperature as the independent variable, the isobar in
@fig-isobaravt25072 show the expanding area-per-particle as the
temperature increases.

```{r}
#| label: fig-isobaravt2507
#| eval: true
#| output: true
#| fig-cap: 'Isobar of @fig-isobar2507 with axes reversed (temperature as independent variable).  The expansion of the substance with temperature while under constant pressure is clear.'
with( S3DTdiff2, {
  n <- 5 # current potential exponent
  P2 <- isob # near transition pressure at 1/pi density
  T2 <- ke.mean.rs * (P2 / Pressure.mean.rs)^(n / (n + 2))
  den2 <- (1 / pi) * (T2 / ke.mean.rs)^(2/n)
  plotconf( y = (1 / den2), x = T2, Fval = Fval, linethresh = 200, 
            panel.first = grid(), ylab = "Area / Particle", 
            xlab = "Temperature",  #xlim = c( 3.0, 3.5)
            main = " Isobar at P = 0.1075"
            )
  axis( side = 1, at = pi, labels = expression(pi))
})
pl <- recordPlot()
png("isobaravt2507.png", width=600, height=300)
replayPlot(pl)
invisible(dev.off())
```

# Next Steps

The basics of the 1979 work have been replicated, except for heating and
cooling. The heating-cooling code does not add any further randomness to
the phase space sampling, although the many initializations already have
that covered. In short, each initialization is a unique instance off
phase space, admittedly with a start at the unlikely instance of minimum
potential energy. There is reason to fear that this starting point may
bias results, and heating and cooling will not change that bias.

The path will be to do four series each of heating and cooling, all
starting from configurations that are considered validly in equilibrium.

# Epilog

On 25 July, I realized that the initial filtering of `MD2DF.L` only
captured the "S3" series, missing the "S3b" data. The additional data
was mostly \~4M+ point runs just above the transition region that were
for the most part not considered valid. The text above has been updated
to include the "S3b" data, which is now included in the `S3DTdiff2` data
table. The "S3b" data was not used in the original analysis, but it is
included here for completeness.
